tasks.title: Section A: Landslides
tasks.statement: Section A deals with landslides based on a photograph from Viti Levu, Fiji, climatic data, triggers, human activities, environmental/human impacts, and mitigation measures.

parts.question: Which of the locations A–F was most recently affected by a landslide?
Which 4 months have the highest risk of landslides based on the climatic data of Pacific Harbour, Viti Levu, Fiji?
parts.reference: January to April (1m).

parts.question: Identify 6 natural triggers that can cause landslides.
parts.reference: Any reasonable list of different triggers (not initial conditions like geology, topography (relief) – steepness of slopes or gravity etc.), each correct answer 0.5m. Examples: Weathering, Heavy precipitation, Hydrogeology, Snowmelt, Retreat of glaciers, Flooding, Fluvial erosion, Coastal erosion, Slopes dried out and cleared by fire, Earthquakes and its vibrations, Tectonic movements, Volcanic activity and eruptions, Tsunami, Previous landslides, Fall of a meteorite, The effect of global warming (if direct influence explained).

parts.question: Identify 6 human activities that can cause landslides.
parts.reference: Any reasonable list of different triggers, each correct answer 0.5m. Examples: Removal of vegetation, Interference with or changes to natural drainage, Damming of water, Irrigation, Modification (cutting and filling) of slopes by development (buildings, urbanisation), Modification (cutting and filling) of slopes by roads/railways/tunnels, Vibrations from heavy traffic, Leaking pipes, Mining activities/blasting/excavation, Filling natural river beds with soil, Inadequate agricultural practices, Recreational activities, Climate changes caused by human activities (CO2 emission), Nuclear weapons testing blasts, War (bombing).

parts.question: Give 3 ways in which a landslide can cause damage to the environment and to people.
parts.reference: Any reasonable list of different damages no matter the category. Examples: Fatalities (killing people and animals), Damage (engulfing people, animals, crops and buildings; cutting off infrastructure; ruining economic viability), Secondary effects (alteration of landscape/damming rivers, landslide dam outburst floods, tsunamis, reef damage due to soil erosion).

parts.question: Outline 2 measures that can reduce the possibility of landslides occurring.
parts.reference: Level marking. Measures should cover avoiding landslide-prone areas, stabilisation of slope (geometric, hydrogeological, mechanical methods), preserving vegetation (reforestation), improving surface and subsurface drainage, constructing piles and retaining walls, rock fall protection, removal and replacement (altering the slope gradient), and legal approach (land use regulation).

tasks.title: Section B: Tsunamis
tasks.statement: Section B covers tsunamis, their causes via earthquakes, travel times, coastal vegetation protection against tsunamis, and economic impacts of marine waste.

parts.question: Draw an annotated diagram(s) to show how a tsunami can be caused by an earthquake.
parts.reference: Submarine earthquake (1m), Displaced column of water (1m), Increasing wave height (and lower speed) towards shore (1m), Annotation (different from labelling) (1m).

parts.question:
a) Provide the coordinates of the point A.
b) If the tsunami occurred at 06:57 GMT at the location marked by point A, what time would it reach point B on the map?
Describe the relationship between the area of coastal vegetation and human death toll based on the Tamil Nadu data from the 2004 tsunami.
parts.reference: Main point: inverse relationship: greater the area of coastal vegetation, the lesser the human death toll from the correlation line on the graph (1m). Any additional reasonable comment with referring to specific numbers where necessary (1m).

parts.question: Explain 2 ways in which the establishment or maintenance of coastal vegetation can aid in tsunami hazard management.
parts.reference: Level marking. Ways include: Reflect and resist tsunami energy (reduce inundation depth, area, current); stop driftwood and other materials; prevent people from being washed out to sea; reduce erosion of beaches and dunes; mangroves act as sinks for suspended sediments.

parts.question: Explain the effect of illegally dumped radioactive nuclear waste brought onto Somalia's coast by the 2004 tsunami on Somalia's economy.
parts.reference: Level marking. Significant pollution of coastal waters ruined local marine life causing the fishing industry to collapse, resulting in loss of jobs/income, rise of piracy, health risks, spending money on cleaning waste instead of development, fewer tourists, and reduced foreign investment.

tasks.title: Section C: Phewa Lake in Nepal
tasks.statement: Section C involves map work, contour interpretation, profiling, and environmental analysis around Phewa Lake in Nepal.

parts.question: Estimate the height of the surface of Phewa Lake based on Figure C1.
parts.reference: Any number or range between 761–800 m above sea level (1m). Answers above 820 m marked 0m.

parts.question: Estimate the length of the perimeter of Phewa Lake based on Figure C1.
Draw a labelled profile of the transect A–B using both Figure C1 and Figure C2.
parts.reference: Elevation (shape) of the profile line (2m, max 1 minor mistake = 1m); Labelling land use and lake (1m); Proper labelling of units of Y-axis (1m).

parts.question: Describe the changes in the area of Phewa Lake between 1988 and 2012 based on Figure C3.
parts.reference: Lake reduced in size (0.5m), approximately 300,000–450,000 m² or 5–10% (0.5m). Separation into two lakes; non-constant shrinking with larger shrinking rate in 1988–1999/2003; reduced on the western side (1m).

parts.question: Explain how the land use surrounding Phewa Lake can affect the lake in 2 ways, using Figure C2.
parts.reference: Level marking. Land use (0.5m) + affect (0.5m) + link/explanation (1m). Examples: surrounding degraded forests lead to runoff and sedimentation; cultivated hill slopes lead to fertilizer runoff and eutrophication; protected forests positively affect water quality.

parts.question: Evaluate the impact of recreational development on Phewa Lake area.
parts.reference: Level marking. Holistic appraisal of potential problems and opportunities (positive/negative impacts) for the area and inhabitants, considering economic benefits vs environmental impacts, time period (short/long term), scale, and developing country context. 1m for at least two well-explained reasons including socio-economic; 2m for classified/labelled impacts from different aspects with contrasting conjunctions; 3m for comparison/weighted conclusion or in-depth geographical analysis.

tasks.title: Section D: Wind Speed
tasks.statement: Section D explores wind speeds, sailing ship routes, flight routes utilizing jet streams, wind turbine power output curves, regional high wind speeds, and meteorological phenomena like tip jets.

parts.question: Describe where and explain why sailing ships experienced the highest (wind) speeds.
parts.reference: Area: 40–60°S, southern part of Indian, Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, Southern Ocean (0.5m). Reason: Occurrence of strong western winds, Westerlies, Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties (1m); no large landmasses to slow down/disrupt wind speed (1m).

parts.question: Describe where and explain why sailing ships experienced decreased (wind) speeds.
parts.reference: Area 1: Horse latitudes (~30°N and ~30°S) (0.5m). Reason: Calm/weak winds in tropical highs, between trade winds and Westerlies (1m). Area 2: Around the equator, doldrums (0.5m). Reason: Calm/weak winds associated with Intertropical Convergence Zone (1m).

parts.question:
a) Explain why route A is usually used when flying from America to Asia.
b) Explain why route B is usually used when flying from Asia to America.
parts.reference:
a) Route A is the shortest (corresponding to orthodrome/great circle) (1m).
b) Route B corresponds to the location of jet stream (from west to east) taking less time and fuel despite being longer (1m).

parts.question:
a) What is the minimum wind speed necessary for a wind turbine to produce electricity?
b) Specify in which wind conditions a wind turbine can produce the greatest power output.
c) Why is no electricity produced at very high wind speeds?
parts.reference:
a) 2–3 or ~2.5 m/s (0.5m).
b) Wind speed 12–25 m/s (0.5m), steady, not variable wind (1m total).
c) Blades are automatically blocked to prevent storm damage (1m).

parts.question: Explain why the mean wind speed in the area indicated by arrow A (Caspian Sea) is significantly higher than in surrounding regions.
parts.reference: Flat surface of the water allows wind to blow with higher speed than surrounding regions with greater terrain roughness (moderately hilly/mountainous) (1m).

parts.question: Give 3 reasons why the area indicated by arrow B (Western Sahara) is not used for the location of wind farms despite having high mean wind speed.
parts.reference: Any reasonable list of different reasons. Natural reasons: Sahara low demand due to nomad population, sandstorms damage (1m). Resource/economic reasons: oil and phosphates in area bringing profit, no need/expertise/know-how for large electricity-intensive industries, LEDC-associated reasons (1m). Political reasons: unstable political situation (e.g., Western Sahara), entrepreneurs unlikely to develop electrical networks/infrastructure over long distances (1m).

parts.question: Explain why Greenland hosts some of the strongest winds on the planet, called tip jets, despite not being known for hurricanes.
parts.reference: Tip jets occur when cyclones meet landmass (obstacle), causing air flow to be distorted and winds to speed up to gale-force. Air parcels going around Greenland have a longer path than those going over it and accelerate to meet at the end (Bernoulli effect) (2m). Accept pressure differences over ice cap vs coast/ocean (1m).

tasks.title: Section E: Population Trends and Challenges
tasks.statement: Section E covers global population growth acceleration post-1950, family planning policies, ageing populations in developed countries, drawing and analyzing the population pyramid of the UAE.

parts.question: Give 2 reasons why total world population growth accelerated significantly after 1950.
parts.reference: Development of new medical insights / improved public health care influencing mortality decline; improved living conditions/standard (hygiene); increased food production in developed countries enabling effective help to developing countries.

parts.question: Suggest 4 measures which a fast growing population / country should include in its Family Planning Policy in order to control its population growth in the future.
parts.reference: Encourage education and awareness about birth control, especially in rural areas; award scholarships for education, especially of girls; improve economic, health, and living conditions; raise marriageable age for men and women; suggest 1-child or 2-child family policy; create public campaigns via TV, radio, newspapers.

parts.question: Outline 2 positive implications of an ageing population in developed countries.
parts.reference: Old retired persons can do part-time work (greater skills and experience); old retired persons can contribute through voluntary work/services; grandparents often provide free (unpaid) childcare.

parts.question: Draw United Arab Emirates' (UAE) population pyramid showing the share (%) of the population using Resource Booklet Table E1.
parts.reference: Labelling Y-axis ('Age group(s)') or writing between columns (0.5m); labelling X-axis ('% of population' or '%') (0.5m); inserting legend or writing 'M' and 'F' (0.5m); correct positioning of male (left) and female (right) (0.5m); correctly locating '0' point on X-axis (1m); correctly drawing male columns (1m) and female columns (1m).

parts.question: Suggest a reason for the unbalanced age and sex structure of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) population, and explain the underlying cause(s) behind that, using Tables E1, E2 and the pyramid.
parts.reference: Level marking. Unbalanced age and sex ratio occurred due to international migration (very high net immigration) — many younger economically active foreigners came to work in oil fields and construction sites. The majority were men and arrived unaccompanied by families.

tasks.title: Section F: Urban Theories and Development
tasks.statement: Section F covers urban development models, characteristics of central urban zones, matching street block layouts with urban fingerprints, urban spatial structure and energy efficiency, and disadvantages of the 'smart city' concept.

parts.question: Describe the urban development in each of the 3 models (A, B, C).
parts.reference: Model A (Concentric zone model): City expands outwards in rings with different land uses; CBD in center surrounded by industry/low-income housing, medium/high-income on periphery (1m). Model B (Sector model): City core in middle, outward progression radially along transport/communication corridors; less desirable zones closer to center witness decaying housing (1m). Model C (Multiple nuclei model): Multimodal urban development in urban sprawl environment where core loses importance and new industrial parks/suburbs form outside, potentially forming new cores/edge cities (1m).

parts.question:
a) Which area/zone (1–10) in the urban development models does the picture of Barcelona (Figure F1) correspond to?
b) What are 3 main characteristics of this area/zone?
parts.reference:
a) '1' (0.5m).
b) 3 characteristics (3 x 0.5m = 1.5m): higher urban density; good infrastructure/accessibility; newest technologies/design; higher land prices/rent; high-income workers; higher concentration of offices and retail buildings (business rather than housing); government offices; tallest buildings/modern outlook; cultural diversity; big daytime, limited night time population.

parts.question: Match the street block layouts (A, B, C and D) with the corresponding urban 'fingerprints' graphs (1, 2, 3 and 4).
parts.reference: Each correct answer 0.5m (4 x 0.5m = 2m): A corresponds to graph 2; B corresponds to graph 4; C corresponds to graph 1; D corresponds to graph 3.

parts.question: Discuss how urban (spatial) structure influences energy efficiency in cities.
parts.reference: Level marking. Urban form and transport systems are two major components. Spatial structure determines energy demand/consumption (transport, space heating/cooling) and opportunities for alternative energy systems. Dense, compact, diverse and concentrated cities reduce travel needs (car use) and lower transport energy use, facilitating 'green transport'. Dispersed urban settlements with physical separation of activities and longer commutes increase travel needs and energy requirements.

parts.question: Elaborate how the 'smart city' concept of future urban development can be disadvantageous for cities.
parts.reference: Level marking. Can contribute to social differences/gap between poor and rich; high-tech methods make cities more expensive; can increase sophisticated corruption; modern technology can lead to city services being shut down or personal information leaked/spying; possible 'domino effect' where interconnected sectors mean failure in one leads to problems in others.
